src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: `@PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id` hands id creation to the database, which is a persistence concern.
src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: `@Column()` on orderId and amount maps the fields to columns, which is ORM mapping that belongs in infrastructure.
src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: `hasId()` only checks whether the database has assigned an id. The file contains no business rules or invariants of its own.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts is in the domain layer, but its class mostly defines how invoices are stored in the database. That is persistence work, which belongs to the infrastructure layer. The @Entity('invoices') decorator names the database table. @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') says the database creates the id as a UUID. @Column() maps the orderId and amount fields to columns. The only behaviour, hasId(), just checks whether the database has assigned an id yet. That reflects persistence state, not a business rule. The rubric names persistence logic in a domain file as a failure. The import of typeorm is not judged here because import direction is out of scope; the failure rests on what the file does, which is storage mapping. Confidence is moderate because the layer model puts all *.entity.ts files in the domain layer, so the project may knowingly accept ORM entities as domain objects.
